FLY TYING / BEGINNERS

Your first evening at the vise.

Learn the tools, sort the materials, and tie a fly you can recognize. Start small. Keep the next one simple.

Start here

Quick answer

Start with a San Juan Worm, then try a Woolly Bugger. Buy the materials for one pattern, set up good light, and work toward an open hook eye and secure wraps.

01

Meet the tools

Swipe the table to compare all columns.

ToolWhat you use it forFirst check
ViseHolds the hookClamp the bend without covering the shank.
ScissorsTrim thread, hair, and feathersKeep fine blades away from wire.
BobbinHolds the spool and feeds threadThread should pull smoothly through the tube.
BodkinPlace tiny drops; separate fibersKeep the sharp point clear of your hand.
Hackle pliersGrip a feather tipTest the grip before you wind.
Hair stackerAlign hair tipsRemove the soft underfur first.
One more useful tool

A whip finisher makes the final knot. Learn its movement on a larger bare hook before you finish a tiny fly.

02

Learn the texture, then the name

Swipe the table to compare all columns.

MaterialLook forIts job here
MarabouSoft, loose fibersA moving Bugger tail.
Pheasant tailLong, narrow brown fibersNymph tail, body, and wingcase.
HackleFibers along a feather stemA wrapped feather collar or body.
ChenilleA fuzzy cordA Bugger body or worm.
WireA fine metallic strandA rib over the body.
Elk hairStiff, hollow hair tipsA caddis wing.

03

A bench that helps you learn

  • ✓Place the vise on a stable table with light behind your working shoulder.
  • ✓Put a plain background behind the hook.
  • ✓Keep only this pattern’s materials on the bench.
  • ✓Use a small tray for loose hooks and beads.
  • ✓Keep sharp tools and loose hooks away from children and pets.
[1]
04

The same rhythm, one fly at a time

  1. 01

    Read the whole recipe

    Lay out the hook, thread, and materials before you start.

  2. 02

    Start with a thread base

    Trap the tag with crossing wraps. Trim it once the thread holds.

  3. 03

    Add one material

    Use the illustrated state to check what belongs on the hook now.

  4. 04

    Make a secure finish

    Whip finish, cut the thread, and check the eye. Tug each material gently.

When the thread breaks

Hold the loose materials in place, restart the thread, and secure them. If the body becomes bulky, start again on a clean hook.

07

Leave the bench ready for tomorrow

  • ✓Return loose hooks to their labelled box.
  • ✓Remove scraps from the vise and table.
  • ✓Keep feathers and hair dry in closed bags.
  • ✓Cap adhesive and follow its storage label.
  • ✓Save one fly from each session to compare your progress.
A few good questions

Before you head out

Do I need a rotary vise?

No. A stable vise that grips your chosen hook is enough for these lessons.

Will tying save me money?

It depends on how much you buy and tie. Start because you enjoy the work; keep the material list small.

What should my first fly look like?

Aim for secure materials and an open eye. A neat, repeatable shape comes with practice.
